name: Siona
confidence_why: Wheeler & Wheeler 1962 describe Siona stress as phonemic with a basic initial pattern while admitting no good minimal pairs, but Wheeler's fuller grammars (1970, 1987) call stress non-contrastive and predictable from the base, with every base syllable stressed and the strongest stress on the base's second or final syllable, and Bruil 2014 finds no contrastive stress at all in Ecuadorian Siona, so the later reference grammar outweighs the early sketch even though all three Wheeler works come from one fieldworker.

new_statements.translation: 5. Phonemic stress is present in two degrees within the word, which is defined as the minimum elicitable form or such a minimum form extended by unstressed syllables that follow it. Although no minimal stress contrasts have been found, it is a conditioning factor. [...] The basic stress patterns include: (1) Stress on the initial syllable of a word followed by an unstressed syllable or word juncture: [...] (2) Two stressed syllables: [...] (3) Two unstressed syllables, of limited occurrence: [...] Heavy stress appears as a feature of the rhythm dynamics of the phrase group, which is not detailed here (see section 2).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's initial placement (StressTyp2 initial stress): the initial syllable is stressed in all stressed words and pattern (1) is the basic one. But the source adds that stress is analysed as phonemic in two degrees, that some disyllables carry stress on both syllables and a few carry none, so a single culminative initial stress is a simplification; there is no word with non-initial stress only. The 1962 English original (pp. 106-107) says exactly the same. Note the listed open_url (SIL search page) is an automated-access block; the PDF was downloaded from the Internet Archive copy of the SIL LCA file for record 17572.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress comes in two degrees. Three lexical patterns are listed: (1) stress on the initial syllable with the following syllable unstressed (examples in the 1962 English original: /t'ó/ 'just that', /yók'u/ 'canoe', /náhi/ 'he is catching'); (2) both syllables of a disyllable stressed (/ʔóká/ 'firewood', /susí/ 'nettle', /t'aʔt'á/ 'first', /yáyá/ 'termite'); (3) a few disyllables with no stressed syllable (/mɨʔɨ/ 'you', /yɨʔɨ/ 'I'). No good minimal pairs; stress is kept as phonemic because it conditions vowel and consonant allophones. In every word that has stress the initial syllable is stressed; what is lexical is whether a second syllable is also stressed or the word is stressless.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Two degrees are distinguished: ordinary word stress and 'acento fuerte' (heavy stress), the latter a phrase-group peak feature (rhythm dynamics), not a word-level secondary stress. Word-level length-plus-decrescendo appears only on a stressed word-initial syllable followed by an unstressed syllable or juncture (sec. 4, p. 63).
new_statements.exceptions: Pattern (2) disyllables with both syllables stressed; pattern (3) disyllables with no stress, 'de ocurrencia limitada' (the pronouns 'I', 'you'). Vowel length and decrescendo lost in fast speech outside the heavy-stress phrase peaks.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Siona of the upper Putumayo River (Colombia, with a smaller group on the Ecuador side), the dialect known as Siona proper, as opposed to the Macaguaje dialect also called Siona (1962/1975 introduction); the 1970/2002 grammar is explicitly the Colombian Siona. The 1975 chapter appears in an Ecuador volume but is a Spanish translation of the 1962 'Siona phonemics (Western Tucanoan)' with the same data.

new_statements.quote: Stress is non-contrastive, but is analyzed as phonemic because of the conditioning effect it has on adjacent vowels and on the selection of certain allomorphs of stem inflection. Stress occurs obligatorily on all verb stem syllables, all root syllables and various suffix syllables. Some single-syllable morphemes have stressed and unstressed alternates. Stress is not written on the first syllable of a stem or root unless the stem or root is monosyllabic. Stress is reduced on words that do not occupy a nuclear position in the phonological phrase, so that the resultant phonetic effect is the same as in cases where stress does not occur.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees that the first syllable of a stem/root is always stressed (so unwritten), which matches the catalog's initial placement; but it states that stress is non-contrastive and falls on ALL root and verb-stem syllables plus various suffix syllables, i.e. a morphological multiple-stress system rather than a single culminative initial stress. That is a difference of type from StressTyp2's initial stress record, though not of leftmost placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and morphologically determined: every syllable of a verb stem and of a root is stressed, as are various suffix syllables; the first syllable of a stem/root is stressed so predictably that it is left unwritten (unless the root is monosyllabic). Some monosyllabic morphemes have stressed and unstressed alternates. Stress is reduced on words outside the nuclear (peak) position of the phonological phrase, where syllables shorten and intervocalic glottal stop drops (p. 21, examples yɨʔɨ 'I', gɨʔɨ 'louse' in peak vs onset position). Stress also drives morphophonemics (p. 22): glottal-stop intercalation and lenis-to-fortis before a stressed vowel; CVi/CVʔi shorten to CV before a stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described; the two-level effect is phrasal: full stress on the head word in the peak of the phonological phrase, reduced stress on words in onset/offglide position (pp. 20-21).
new_statements.exceptions: Single-syllable morphemes with stressed and unstressed alternates; stress reduction on non-nuclear words in the phonological phrase.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Siona of the upper Putumayo River (Colombia, with a smaller group on the Ecuador side), the dialect known as Siona proper, as opposed to the Macaguaje dialect also called Siona (1962/1975 introduction); the 1970/2002 grammar is explicitly the Colombian Siona. The 1975 chapter appears in an Ecuador volume but is a Spanish translation of the 1962 'Siona phonemics (Western Tucanoan)' with the same data.

readall_conflicts: The two Wheeler works do not contradict each other on placement: both put stress on the initial syllable of every stressed word/root, and the 1975 phonemics' 'two stressed syllables' and 'two unstressed syllables' patterns are what the 1970 grammar restates as 'stress on all root syllables' and 'single-syllable morphemes with stressed and unstressed alternates'. They differ in framing: the 1975 chapter (and its 1962 English original) calls stress 'fonémico' in two degrees while admitting no minimal contrasts; the 1970 grammar says outright 'Stress is non-contrastive, but is analyzed as phonemic' for its conditioning effects. Against the catalog (StressTyp2, single fixed initial stress), both sources agree the initial syllable is stressed but describe a non-culminative, morphologically governed system (every root syllable and various suffixes stressed; a few stressless disyllabic pronouns), so the catalog record is a simplification rather than a wrong placement.

audit.recode_to: From 'lexical' to predictable, morphologically anchored stress (Colombian Siona, Wheeler 1987 I:89-91): primary stress on the final syllable of the base/root (σ2 of 2-syll, σ3 of 3-syll; σ2+σ4 strongest in 4-syll bases, i.e. iambic within the base), all base syllables bearing some stress, suffixes/enclitics alternating unstressed-stressed after the base, a few lexically stressed suffixes. In catalog terms: classification morphological/stem-final (dom = stem, right edge), not lexical; whole-word positional rule still not count-computable ('None ridable' over the word can stand) because suffix strings vary. Add a caution that Ecuadorian Siona (Bruil 2014:86-87) shows only a word-final pitch rise with no demonstrated stress system, so the languoid mixes two differently described varieties. The StressTyp2 'initial' contra note remains valid (neither 1962 nor 1987 supports fixed initial stress).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim at Wheeler & Wheeler 1962:107-108 in the PDF we hold (rendered pp. 12-13). (2) The deciding source is a 1962 SIL phonemics article with a one-paragraph, morphology-blind stress section; the same author's 1987 reference grammar (held but unused: §2.2.3 pp. 89-92, read now from page scan hi-105.108) analyses stress as predictable from the base: strongest stress base-final (iambic σ2/σ4 in 4-syll bases), alternating rhythm over suffixes, stress 'rarely' meaning-distinguishing. That directly undercuts the 'lexical' classification, which was inferred from the 1962 list of three surface patterns (those patterns are base+atonic-suffix vs. disyllabic-base parses under the 1987 analysis). Bruil 2014 §3.2.3 (held) adds that Ecuadorian Siona has no demonstrated stress system, only a word-final pitch rise. (3)
